question: In boating navigation rules, what is a 'stand-on vessel'?
choice_a: The vessel that must always slow down and stop
choice_b: A vessel that is anchored and not moving
choice_d: The vessel that has right-of-way and should maintain its current course and speed
explanation: The stand-on vessel has the right-of-way in a given situation and should hold its course and speed so the give-way vessel can predict its movement and maneuver safely around it.
source_note: Navigation Rules (Inland), stand-on/give-way concept, PA-approved boating courses

question: What is the 'give-way vessel' required to do when meeting another vessel in a crossing or meeting situation?
choice_a: Take early and substantial action to keep clear of the stand-on vessel
choice_b: Speed up to cross in front of the stand-on vessel
choice_c: Ignore the other vessel since size determines right-of-way
choice_d: Wait until a collision is imminent before reacting
explanation: The give-way vessel must take early, obvious action -- usually slowing, stopping, or altering course -- to avoid a collision and stay well clear of the stand-on vessel.

question: When two power-driven vessels are approaching each other head-on, what should both operators do?
choice_b: Each should alter course to starboard (right) so they pass port-to-port, like cars on a road
choice_c: Both should speed up to pass quickly
explanation: In a head-on meeting, both power-driven vessels are considered give-way and should each alter course to starboard, passing each other port side to port side.
source_note: Navigation Rules (Inland), head-on meeting rule, PA-approved boating courses

question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the give-way vessel?
choice_c: The vessel that has the other vessel approaching from its own starboard (right) side
choice_d: The vessel that has the other vessel approaching from its own port (left) side
explanation: When two power-driven vessels are crossing, the vessel that sees the other vessel on its own starboard (right) side must give way; the other vessel is the stand-on vessel and should hold course and speed.
source_note: Navigation Rules (Inland), crossing rule, PA-approved boating courses

question: What is the general rule for an overtaking vessel (one approaching another vessel from more than 22.5 degrees abaft its beam)?
choice_a: The vessel being overtaken must always move out of the way
choice_b: Overtaking vessels always have the right-of-way
choice_c: The rule only applies to sailing vessels
choice_d: The overtaking vessel is always the give-way vessel, regardless of whether it is a power or sail vessel, and must keep clear until safely past
explanation: Any vessel overtaking another, whether a powerboat or a sailboat, is the give-way vessel in that situation and must keep well clear of the vessel being overtaken.
source_note: Navigation Rules (Inland), overtaking rule, PA-approved boating courses

question: In an encounter between a power-driven vessel and a sailing vessel under sail alone, which vessel generally has the right-of-way?
choice_a: The sailing vessel, since it has less maneuverability under wind power alone
choice_b: The power-driven vessel, since it can maneuver more easily
choice_d: Neither vessel has right-of-way over the other
explanation: A sailing vessel under sail is generally the stand-on vessel over a power-driven vessel, since sail power offers less precise maneuverability, though this reverses if the sailboat is overtaking the powerboat.
source_note: Navigation Rules (Inland), power-vs-sail rule, PA-approved boating courses

question: Under Pennsylvania and federal navigation rules, do personal watercraft (PWC) follow the same right-of-way rules as other power-driven vessels?
choice_a: PWC follow sailing vessel rules instead
choice_b: Yes, a PWC is treated as a power-driven vessel and must follow the same navigation rules as other powerboats
choice_c: No, PWC always have the right-of-way over other boats
choice_d: No, PWC are exempt from all navigation rules
explanation: A PWC is legally a power-driven vessel and must obey the same navigation rules -- including stand-on/give-way duties -- as any other motorboat.
source_note: PWC navigation rule application, PA Fish and Boat Commission regulations

question: What should a boat operator do when navigating in conditions of restricted visibility, such as fog on a large lake?
choice_a: Turn off all lights to avoid confusing other boaters
choice_b: Continue at normal cruising speed since radar is not required on small boats
choice_c: Slow to a safe speed, post a lookout, and sound the appropriate fog signals at intervals
choice_d: Increase speed to get through the fog faster
explanation: In restricted visibility, boaters must proceed at a safe speed for conditions, maintain a proper lookout by sight and hearing, and use sound signals to alert nearby vessels of their presence.
source_note: Navigation Rules, restricted-visibility procedures, PA-approved boating courses

question: What is the 'danger zone' or 'zone of danger' in navigation rules for power-driven vessels?
choice_a: Any area within 5 miles of shore
choice_b: The area directly behind a vessel only
choice_c: A zone that only applies to sailing vessels
choice_d: The area from dead ahead to 112.5 degrees abaft the starboard beam of a vessel, within which an approaching vessel is the give-way vessel
explanation: The danger zone extends from dead ahead to 112.5 degrees abaft a vessel's starboard side; if another power-driven vessel approaches from within this zone, that approaching vessel must give way.
source_note: Navigation Rules (Inland), danger zone concept, PA-approved boating courses

question: Which vessel generally has right-of-way over a power-driven recreational vessel due to limited ability to maneuver: a large commercial vessel confined to a marked channel, such as one navigating a Pennsylvania river?
choice_a: The large vessel confined to the channel, because it cannot safely leave the channel to avoid smaller, more maneuverable boats
choice_b: The smaller recreational boat, because smaller boats always have right-of-way
choice_d: Right-of-way is decided by which boat arrived at the channel first
explanation: A vessel restricted by its draft to a narrow channel cannot maneuver out of the way like a smaller boat can, so recreational boaters must stay clear and avoid impeding vessels confined to a marked channel.
source_note: Navigation Rules, vessels constrained by draft/channel, PA-approved boating courses

question: What does one short blast of a horn mean when signaling intentions to a nearby vessel under the Inland Navigation Rules?
choice_a: I intend to leave you on my starboard side
choice_b: I intend to leave you on my port side (I am altering my course to starboard)
choice_c: I am in distress and require immediate assistance
explanation: Under the Inland Rules, one short blast signals 'I intend to leave you on my port side,' meaning the signaling vessel intends to alter course to starboard.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules sound signals, PA-approved boating courses

question: What does five (or more) short, rapid blasts of a horn mean between vessels?
choice_b: It signals nothing in particular and can be ignored
choice_c: Danger signal -- I do not understand your intentions or I disagree with your intended action
choice_d: I am passing on your port side
explanation: Five or more short, rapid blasts is the danger signal, used when an operator does not understand or agrees with another vessel's intentions, or believes the other vessel's action is insufficient to avoid collision.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules sound signals, PA-approved boating courses

question: Even when an operator is the stand-on vessel with right-of-way, what must they still do?
choice_a: Nothing -- the stand-on vessel bears no responsibility for avoiding a collision
choice_b: Speed up to clear the area faster
choice_d: Continue to keep a proper lookout and take action to avoid a collision if the give-way vessel fails to yield in time
explanation: Right-of-way is not absolute; a stand-on vessel must still keep a lookout and take last-resort evasive action if the give-way vessel does not yield in time to avoid a collision.
source_note: Navigation Rules, stand-on vessel responsibility, PA-approved boating courses

question: What is the responsibility of every vessel operator regarding lookout, under the navigation rules?
choice_a: Maintain a proper lookout by sight and hearing at all times to assess the risk of collision
choice_b: Only maintain a lookout when other boats are visible
choice_c: Delegate lookout duty entirely to passengers with no responsibility on the operator
choice_d: Lookout is only required at night
explanation: Every operator must maintain a proper lookout using both sight and hearing at all times, appropriate to the conditions, to fully assess the risk of collision with other vessels, swimmers, or obstructions.
source_note: Navigation Rules, proper lookout requirement, PA-approved boating courses
